fact: The World Bank's identity diagnostic states that MASSAR was developed by the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFP) over two and a half years and officially launched at the end of 2013; it gives no spending figure for it.

The diagnostic states that MASSAR's student register covers every child enrolled in any of the more than 10,000 national educational establishments, ages 6 to 18: 6,512,192 unique students as of May 2014, about 94 per cent of the 6.9 million children of that age, and by the World Bank's reckoning 98 per cent of children of primary age (6 to 10).

The diagnostic describes MASSAR as a fully electronic system for managing 'all aspects of the scholastic life' of children, in which each establishment registers and vets its own students into a central, cumulative database and each student receives a unique number kept for the whole of their schooling, with about 600,000 new entrants a year; it does not say that attendance or results are entered (assessment visit of June 2014).

The diagnostic states that MASSAR's central database is reached by secure access from 10,000 locations and that students are vetted at each of the country's 10,000 learning establishments, a figure for all levels aged 6 to 18 with no separate count of primary schools and no rural breakdown (assessment visit of June 2014).

The ministry's letter of 7 May 2026 says that in the pioneer middle schools teachers record pupils' absence at the start of each lesson and the school administration keys it into the 'Massar+ Idara' application, validates it and classes each absence as justified or not, for daily and real-time monitoring.
The ministry's letter of 7 May 2026 applies daily absence entry in 'Massar+ Idara' to lower secondary schools (the 'pioneer' middle schools, i'dadiyat al-riyada); it does not mention primary schools.

The ministry's letter of 7 May 2026 rolls out a 'new digital component' for daily, real-time monitoring of pupil absence in pioneer middle schools through 'Massar+ Idara', following its letter no. 1931/26 of 6 May 2026 institutionalising that monitoring.

The letter of 7 May 2026 is the Ministry of National Education, Preschool and Sports' own instruction to the regional academies, signed by its secretary-general, setting who records and who validates absence in 'Massar+ Idara'.

The national evaluation body (INE, CSEFRS) says in its 2019 atlas that MASSAR was designed as a school management system covering all schools, public and private, from preschool onwards, and it follows real cohorts of primary pupils through to lower secondary from MASSAR's individual records for 2014-2018.

The 2019 atlas says MASSAR holds a record per pupil under a unique pupil identifier for each school year and has a pupil assessment component from which marks reports are issued and through which parents consult their children's marks online; the passages read do not say who keys the marks.

The 2019 atlas describes MASSAR, adopted in 2013, as in service and its pupil cohorts as exhaustive, but gives no count or share of primary schools entering data; 'all schools' is stated as what the platform was designed to cover.
The 2019 atlas says MASSAR was created by the Ministry of National Education to ease school management, and that the ministry supplied the INE with re-coded pupil identifiers for the study.
